group: Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk
question:
Patient note:
A 72-year-old man presented to the pre-operative medicine service this morning for assessment before next month’s scheduled open repair of a 5.9-cm infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm that will be approached through a transperitoneal midline incision with anticipated cross-clamp time of about an hour and an expected intensive care unit stay post-operatively. He arrived walking slowly with a rolling walker, stating that over the last year he can manage two flights of stairs if he pauses midway, but when he tries to mow half his lawn without stopping he develops mild ankle puffiness and needs to catch his breath; he sleeps on two pillows and gained three pounds of water weight during a recent weekend trip but responded promptly to an extra dose of his loop diuretic. The cardiology record documents a hospitalization ten months ago for acute decompensation marked by orthopnea and bibasilar crackles, during which a transthoracic echocardiogram showed a left ventricular ejection fraction of 30 % with diffuse hypokinesis. He has been stable since discharge on carvedilol 25 mg twice daily, sacubitril-valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, and furosemide 40 mg each morning; his last clinic note four weeks earlier described no paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea and only trace pedal edema. Coronary disease was first identified eight years ago after an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction treated with two drug-eluting stents to the right coronary artery; he completed cardiac rehabilitation, remains on dual antiplatelet therapy with low-dose aspirin and clopidogrel, and denies exertional chest pressure, jaw discomfort, presyncope, or palpitations since. A nuclear stress test performed six months ago to guide aneurysm surgery planning demonstrated a fixed inferolateral defect consistent with scar and no inducible ischemia at 7 metabolic equivalents; baseline ECG today again shows Q waves in leads III and aVF without acute ST-T changes. His medical history also includes long-standing hypertension, stage 4 chronic kidney disease attributed to ischemic nephropathy with a baseline serum creatinine of 2.0 mg/dL drawn this morning, dyslipidemia managed with high-intensity rosuvastatin, and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus for which he takes metformin 500 mg twice daily but has never used injectable glucose-lowering agents. He has no personal history of stroke, transient focal neurologic events, or carotid intervention, and a carotid duplex obtained last year was unremarkable. Surgical history is limited to an uncomplicated laparoscopic appendectomy in his twenties. He quit smoking fifteen years ago following a 40-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of bourbon on weekends, and does not use illicit substances. Current medications, in addition to those mentioned, include spironolactone 25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, lisinopril 10 mg each morning, omeprazole 20 mg for reflux, and cholecalciferol 1,000 IU daily; no drug allergies are reported. Family history is notable for a father who died of myocardial infarction at 60 and a sister with congestive heart failure, but no known aneurysms. Review of systems is negative for fever, weight loss, abdominal pain, claudication, syncope, or visual disturbances. On examination he appears euvolemic and in no distress. Vital signs seated: blood pressure 118/66 mm Hg in the right arm, heart rate 72 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 per minute, temperature 36.6 °C, and oxygen saturation 96 % breathing ambient air; body mass index is 27 kg/m². The jugular venous pulsation is measured at 7 cm above the sternal angle, carotid upstrokes are brisk without bruit, the point of maximal impulse is displaced laterally, and auscultation reveals a soft S3 with a grade 1/6 apical holosystolic murmur but no pericardial rub. Lungs are clear except for faint late inspiratory crackles at both bases. Abdomen is protuberant yet soft, revealing a pulsatile midline mass without tenderness; femoral and distal pulses are symmetrical. There is 1+ pitting edema at the ankles. Neurologic screening shows alert mentation, intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength, normal sensation, and steady gait with the walker. Pre-operative laboratory results obtained an hour before the visit reveal sodium 137 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 24 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 38 mg/dL, creatinine 2.0 mg/dL, hemoglobin 12.4 g/dL, platelet count 210 × 10³/µL, and fasting glucose 108 mg/dL; liver function tests are within reference ranges and international normalized ratio is 1.1. Chest radiograph demonstrates mild cardiomegaly and clear lung fields. Airway evaluation notes a Mallampati class III oropharynx with good cervical extension and dentition intact. The vascular surgery team plans to continue the beta-blocker through the morning of surgery, hold the angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor on the day of operation to mitigate intra-operative hypotension, administer half the usual diuretic dose the evening before, and resume clopidogrel after epidural catheter removal on postoperative day three. He has been counseled extensively on smoking abstinence, incentive spirometry, renal protective strategies including pre-operative hydration, and the risks of cardiac decompensation, renal failure possibly necessitating dialysis, bleeding, graft infection, and lower-extremity ischemia. The patient voices understanding of the peri-operative plan and affirms his wish to proceed with definitive aneurysm repair.

Question: What is the patient's score of the Revised Cardiac Risk Index for Pre-Operative Risk? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) assigns one point for each of six preoperative risk factors:
- High-risk surgery: planned open transperitoneal aortic aneurysm repair → 1.
- Ischemic heart disease: prior inferior STEMI, even though the recent stress test showed no inducible ischemia → 1.
- History of heart failure: prior decompensation with LVEF 30% → 1.
- Cerebrovascular disease: no prior stroke or TIA → 0.
- Preoperative insulin treatment: takes metformin, not insulin → 0.
- Serum creatinine >2.0 mg/dL: exactly 2.0 mg/dL does not exceed the threshold → 0.
Total = 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 3.
Final answer: 3
